title: What the Talmud is
hookLine: the Mishnah, gathered around 200 CE, and centuries of discussion around it, printed with commentaries on every side

cards: Picture a page unlike any other. In the middle, a small block of text. Wrapped around it, on the inside edge, a column in a different typeface.

On the outside edge, another. Around those, smaller notes, cross-references, tiny letters in the margins. It looks like a city seen from the air: an old town in the center, neighborhoods growing out in every direction.
That's a page of Talmud. For the next few weeks, i'll give you a taste of it. And the first surprise: you've already been reading part of it.

teach.b: Start with the old town in the center. Remember Rabbi Judah the Prince, who taught that small commandments count? Around the year two hundred, he gathered generations of oral teaching into one book, the Mishnah.

It has six orders: farming and blessings, festivals, marriage and family, damages, holy things, and purity. Pirkei Avot, the sayings you just finished, is one small tractate of it. Then the rabbis kept talking.

For the next few centuries, in the academies of the land of Israel and of Babylonia, they studied every line of the Mishnah and argued over it, in Hebrew and mostly in Aramaic. That discussion is the Gemara.
Mishnah plus Gemara: the Talmud. There are two. The Jerusalem Talmud, from the land of Israel, and the larger Babylonian Talmud, the one most people mean.
The word comes from the Hebrew root for learning and teaching. Here's what makes it unlike most holy books. It keeps the arguments.

teach.h: BOTH OPINIONS STAY ON THE PAGE.
teach.b: When two sages disagree, both opinions stay on the page, often with the losing side's reasons carefully preserved. Of the schools of Hillel and Shammai, the Talmud says: these and these are the words of the living God.

When it was printed in Venice in the fifteen-twenties, the layout put Rashi's commentary on the inner edge and the Tosafot, later scholars from France and Germany, on the outer. Later editions added more.
One page, voices from many centuries, all talking at once.

how: Many Jews study Talmud in pairs (chavruta), reading aloud and arguing through each passage, in yeshivas, synagogues, and study groups; some learn one page every day.

games.q: you're editing a holy book. two great sages disagree, and the law follows one of them. what do you do with the other opinion?
o: keep it on the page, with its reasons.
mention it in a footnote, unnamed.
games.why: the Talmud keeps both, and says of Hillel's school and Shammai's: these and these are the words of the living God.

practice: Imagine the small block at the center of the page: a question someone asked almost two thousand years ago.

Around it, a sage answering, another disagreeing, and Rashi, a French commentator nearly nine hundred years later, writing in the margin. At the very edge there's room for you; what question would you add?
